lessons.title: What Are Transaction Costs and Slippage, and Why Do They Break Backtests?

children.text: Run a backtest on five years of Nifty 500 data for a systematic long-short strategy and it is common to see numbers that look almost too good: 18 to 25 percent CAGR, a Sharpe ratio above 1.5, drawdowns that stay within a comfortable band. Take the exact same rules live, route the same signals through a real broker, and the number that shows up in your contract notes six months later is often a fraction of what the backtest promised. Nothing about the strategy logic changed. What changed is that the backtest quietly assumed a version of the market that does not exist, one where every trade fills at exactly the price on the chart, for free. This lesson is about the two things that close that gap, transaction costs and slippage, and why almost every backtest built without them is measuring a strategy that cannot actually be traded.
Two Numbers, One Strategy: What the Backtest Shows vs What You Actually Earn

Every backtest produces what is best thought of as a gross return, the return a strategy would earn in a world with no cost of trading at all. What actually lands in your demat and trading account is a net return, the gross return minus everything the market and the broker charge to execute the trades. For a strategy that barely trades, a buy-and-hold portfolio rebalanced once a year, the gap between the two numbers can be small enough to ignore. For a strategy that turns over its entire portfolio every week or every day, which describes most of what quant analyst aspirants and prop desks actually build, that gap is not a rounding error. It can be the entire difference between a strategy worth trading and one that quietly loses money at scale.

body.text: A backtest that reports gross returns and calls it a day is not lying exactly, it is answering a question nobody asked: what would this strategy have earned in a market with no transaction costs and no slippage? That market does not exist on the NSE, the BSE, or anywhere else.

children.text: Transaction Costs: The Charges You Can Look Up Before You Trade

markDefs.definition: The explicit, published charges levied on every trade: broker brokerage, STT, stamp duty, exchange transaction charges, SEBI turnover fees, and GST on top of the broker's fees.

children.text: are the explicit, quotable charges attached to every trade you place in the Indian market: broker brokerage, the Securities Transaction Tax (STT), stamp duty, exchange transaction charges, SEBI turnover fees, and GST on top of the broker's fees. Every one of these has a published rate. A Zerodha or Groww user can look up the exact brokerage slab and STT rate before placing a single order. Because they are known in advance, transaction costs are the easier half of the cost problem to model correctly in a backtest, and Chapter 2 builds that model line by line.
Slippage: The Cost the Market Charges You After the Fact

markDefs.definition: The gap between the price a trade was expected to fill at and the price it actually filled at, driven by bid-ask spread and market impact.

children.text: is the gap between the price you expected to pay or receive when you decided to trade and the price you actually got once the order was filled. It has no published rate card because it depends on how liquid the specific stock or contract is at that exact moment, how wide the bid-ask spread is, and how large your order is relative to what the order book can absorb without moving. A market order to buy 50 shares of Reliance Industries during normal trading hours barely registers. The same logic executed at twenty times the size in a thinly traded small-cap stock can move the price several percent against you before the order is fully filled. Chapter 3 breaks slippage down into its two components, spread cost and market impact, and shows how to model both.

body.title: Two Very Different Kinds of Cost

columns.label: Transaction Costs (Explicit)
points: Published rate card: brokerage, STT, stamp duty, exchange charges, GST
Identical for every trader using the same broker and instrument
Known with certainty before you place the order
Straightforward to code into a backtest as a fixed formula

columns.label: Slippage (Implicit)
points: No published rate, it depends on the market at that moment
Different for every trader depending on order size and liquidity
Only known for certain after the trade has filled
Requires a model, and the model can still be wrong

children.text: Why the Gap Widens the More a Strategy Trades

Both costs share one property that matters enormously for backtesting: they are charged per trade, not per rupee of profit. A strategy that rebalances once a month pays this tax twelve times a year. A strategy that rebalances daily pays it roughly twenty times more often. If the average round trip costs even 0.15 to 0.25 percent of trade value once transaction costs and slippage are combined, a daily strategy can be handing back several percentage points of CAGR every year before a single rupee of alpha is counted. This is the single most common reason a strategy that looks brilliant on paper turns mediocre, or unprofitable, once it starts trading turnover it cannot afford.

body.title: Illustrative Gross vs Net CAGR by Rebalancing Frequency

children.text: The chart is illustrative, not drawn from a specific published strategy, but the shape is exactly what shows up again and again in practice. Gross returns often look better as trading frequency increases, more trades usually means more chances to capture short-term edges. Net returns tell a different story. Past a certain point, each additional trade adds more cost than it adds edge, and the strategy that looked best on paper can end up the worst once you are honest about what it actually costs to trade.

children.text: Ask around any desk of quant analyst aspirants preparing for interviews and you will hear some version of the same story: a strategy backtested to a 20 percent plus CAGR that returned closer to mid single digits, or lost money outright, once it went live. It is such a common pattern that it has become something of a rite of passage. The next lesson works through exactly this scenario end to end, a real-style case study showing precisely where the returns went, so the pattern stops being a cautionary tale you have heard about and becomes one you know how to diagnose.

children.text: Where This Course Goes From Here

This course builds the cost discipline that separates a backtest you can trust from one that flatters you. Chapter 2 prices the full Indian transaction cost stack and shows how to code it into a backtest. Chapter 3 does the same for slippage, covering spread cost and market impact. Chapter 4 quantifies exactly how a strategy's turnover determines its sensitivity to both, and introduces break-even analysis. Chapter 5 turns all of this into a checklist for building backtests that do not lie to you. The capstone chapter closes with the transition from backtest to live capital, and the cost and slippage questions that come up in quant and prop trading interviews.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: A strategy shows a 20% CAGR in a backtest. Once real transaction costs and slippage are applied, the same strategy shows a 9% CAGR live. Which is the most accurate description of what happened?
options: The strategy's underlying logic became less accurate over time
The gross edge in the backtest was real, but a large share of it was consumed by the cost of actually executing the trades
The backtest period had unusually favorable market conditions that will not repeat
The live broker used a different price data source than the backtest
body.explanation: Nothing about the strategy's signal generation needs to have changed for this gap to appear. It is the expected, structural consequence of a backtest that assumed frictionless trading meeting a market that charges transaction costs and imposes slippage on every trade. The rest of this course is about quantifying and controlling that gap.

body.text: A backtest without transaction costs and slippage is not measuring your strategy, it is measuring a strategy that trades in a market that does not exist. Every rupee your strategy earns has to survive contact with brokerage, STT, spread, and market impact before it is real money, and the more often the strategy trades, the more of that survival test it has to pass.

points: A backtest's gross return and your actual net return are two different numbers, and the gap between them is transaction costs plus slippage, not strategy decay.
Transaction costs (brokerage, STT, stamp duty, exchange charges, GST) are explicit and known in advance; slippage (spread cost and market impact) is implicit and only known after the trade fills.
Both costs are charged per trade, so the gap between gross and net returns widens as a strategy's turnover increases, not as its capital increases.
A 30 to 70 percent shrinkage between backtested and live CAGR is a common, expected pattern for high-turnover strategies, not a sign that something unusual went wrong.
